Neuroradiology

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Look at a brain image and say whether it is a CT or an MRI (and, for MRI, which sequence) by reading which tissues are bright and which are dark.
  2. LO 2Apply the core rules of neuroimaging: how CT density and MRI signal work, which study to order first, when contrast helps or hurts, and how edema type, diffusion and enhancement point to a diagnosis.
  3. LO 3Recognize the common intracranial diseases on CT and MRI: the four hemorrhages, ischemic stroke, mass effect and herniation, meningeal disease, and a brain mass.

MAPBig picture

  • Every study costs money + risk → ask why → will it change management?
  • CT → density only → fast, everywhere → first study for anything acute (bleed, mass effect, hydrocephalus, edema)
  • MRI → hydrogen proton signal
    • T1 likes fat · T2 loves fluid
    • FLAIR · fat-sat · DWI · gadolinium → normal goes dark → disease lights up
  • Pattern + history → name the pathology (same image → meningitis or carcinomatosis)

LO 1CT or MRI? Which sequence?Read the brightness of bone, CSF, fat, gray and white matter

By the end: you can name any axial brain image as CT, T1, T2, FLAIR, FLAIR + fat-sat or DWI in under 10 seconds, and explain why each tissue looks the way it does.
Q1. What is a CT actually measuring?
  • CT (computed tomography) sends ionizing radiation (x-rays) through the head and measures how much each voxel attenuates (blocks) the beam.
    • More attenuation = denser = whiter. Air blocks nothing → black.
    • That is the only thing CT knows → "one-trick pony": it depends only on the density of the object.
  • The density scale (Hounsfield units, HU) is anchored on water = 0. Less dense than water → negative; denser → positive. Air is the least dense (black).
  • Vocabulary: hyperdense (brighter), hypodense (darker), isodense (same as brain). Never "hyperintense" on CT.
  • On a head CT you see 4 densities: bone, gray matter, white matter, CSF (plus scalp soft tissue).
CheckWhy is an acute hemorrhage bright on CT but CSF dark?
Clotted blood is packed with protein (hemoglobin) → 55–75 HU, denser than brain (~22–45). CSF is nearly water (0–10 HU), less dense than brain → dark.
Step 1 trap — wrong vocabulary

CT findings are dense (hyper/hypodense); MRI findings are intense (hyper/hypointense, "signal"). An answer choice that calls a CT bleed "hyperintense" is mixing modalities.

Memory tool — D vs I

CT Counts Density. MRI Measures Intensity. If the word is "density", you are on CT.

Q2. Why is gray matter brighter than white matter on CT, and what does it mean when that difference disappears?

Gray matter (cortex, deep nuclei)

  • Packed with neuronal cell bodies → denser
  • Hyperdense (brighter) vs WM
  • High metabolic demand → first to suffer in ischemia

White matter (tracts)

  • Myelinated axons; myelin is fat (lipid)
  • Fat is hypodense → WM is darker than GM
  • Rule: GM should always be slightly brighter than WM
Ischemiablood supply cut off
→
No ATPmitochondria cannot supply it
→
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase failspump in the plasma membrane stops
→
Gray matter swellswater enters cells
→
GM looks like WMloss of GM/WM differentiation
  • Loss of gray–white differentiation = the cortex has swollen and become as dark as the white matter. Causes to know: stroke, seizure, infection.
  • In early MCA stroke this shows up as the insular ribbon sign (the insular cortex fades) and an obscured lentiform nucleus.
CheckWhy is the cortex the first place injured when blood flow stops?
Neuronal cell bodies have the highest energy demand. Their Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps need ATP from mitochondria; without ATP the pumps fail, Na⁺ and water flood in, and the gray matter swells first.
Step 1 HY — early CT signs of ischemic stroke
  • CT is often normal in the first hours of an ischemic stroke; its first job is to exclude hemorrhage before thrombolysis.
  • Earliest signs: hyperdense MCA sign (bright clot in the artery), then insular ribbon loss and obscured basal ganglia, then frank hypodensity.
Step 1 trap — where the pump lives

The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase sits in the plasma membrane; mitochondria only supply its ATP. An option placing the pump "in the mitochondria" is wrong.

Q3. How do I sanity-check a normal axial head CT?
  1. Fold it in half. The two hemispheres should be mirror images. Asymmetry → mass effect or midline shift.
  2. The brain should smile at you (at the level of the 3rd ventricle):
    • Eyes = frontal horns of the lateral ventricles
    • Nose = 3rd ventricle
    • Mouth = quadrigeminal (basal) cistern
    • Lost smile → cerebral edema
  3. The 4th ventricle should frown (posterior fossa slice).
    • Lost frown → mass effect
CheckThe frontal horns, 3rd ventricle and basal cisterns are all squeezed shut on a trauma CT. What process is this?
Diffuse cerebral edema: the brain has lost its "smile" because swollen tissue effaces CSF spaces. It is a warning sign for herniation.
Memory tool — the face

The supratentorial brain is happy (smile); the posterior fossa is grumpy (frown). A brain that is no longer happy is swollen; a 4th ventricle that stops frowning is being pushed.

Q4. How does MRI make a picture, and how is it different from CT?
  • "Forget everything you just learned about CT." MRI uses no ionizing radiation, and electron density has no effect on how things look.
  • The patient sits in a strong magnetic field; radio pulses tip hydrogen protons, and the scanner listens as they relax. Different tissues (fat, water, myelin) have different spin behavior → different signal.
  • Vocabulary: hyperintense / hypointense / isointense (signal intensity).
  • Strengths: far better soft-tissue characterization; much more definitive about lesions; special sequences (hemorrhage vs calcification, ultra-thin cuts for cranial nerves, advanced techniques like perfusion and spectroscopy).
  • Weaknesses (every CT pro is an MRI con): slow, expensive, less available, needs more technologists, and patients must be screened for metal (e.g., pacemakers).
CheckCould a bone fragment and a blood clot look identical on MRI even though their densities differ greatly?
Yes in principle: MRI ignores density and reads proton behavior, so brightness depends on the sequence and the tissue's chemistry (water, fat, blood breakdown products), not on how much it blocks x-rays. Cortical bone has almost no mobile protons → dark on every MRI sequence.
Step 1 HY — MRI safety
  • Screen for non-MRI-conditional pacemakers/defibrillators, ferromagnetic aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, and metal fragments in the orbit (metalworkers: get orbital x-rays first).
  • CT radiation matters most in children and pregnancy; MRI is preferred when time allows.
Step 1 trap — "better" is not "first"

MRI is more sensitive for almost everything, but the right first test in an unstable or acutely ill patient is still non-contrast CT (fast, no metal screening, finds blood).

Q5. T1 or T2? The two facts you must memorize

Fact 1 · T1 likes fat

T1 likes fat better than T2 does. Fat (scalp, marrow, orbit, lipoma, myelin) is bright.

Fact 2 · T2 loves fluid

No one loves fluid more than T2. CSF, edema, cysts are bright.

Then look at three things on every MRI: GM vs WM, fluid, and fat. The tissues never change; only the weighting does.

  • White matter is full of myelin (lipid) → T1 likes it → WM brighter than GM on T1 ("looks like a real brain").
  • Gray matter holds more water → T2 likes it → GM brighter than WM on T2 (inverted, "negative" look).
  • Fluid: dark on T1, only bright on T2.
  • Fat: bright on both (brighter on T1).

What is white on which scan?

TissueCT (non-contrast)T1T2FLAIRFLAIR + FS
CSF / simple fluiddarkdarkbrightdark (suppressed)dark
Edema / abnormal fluidhypodensedarkbrightbright (stands out)bright
Fat (scalp, marrow, lipoma)very dark (−100)brightfairly bright (less than fluid)brightdark (suppressed)
White vs gray matterGM brighterWM brighterGM brighterGM brighterGM brighter
Cortical bone / airbone bright, air blackdark on every MRI sequence (few mobile protons)
CheckThe ventricles are white and the cortex is brighter than the white matter. Which sequence?
T2. Bright fluid can only be T2 (T2 loves fluid), and GM > WM fits T2.
CheckOn which sequence is white matter brighter than gray matter, and why?
T1, because white matter is rich in myelin (fat) and T1 likes fat.
Memory tool — WW2 and the fat burger
  • "World War 2": Water is White on T2.
  • T1 = 1 fat burger; T2 = H₂O.
  • T1 "looks like the brain you dissected" (WM pale, ventricles dark); T2 "looks like a photo negative".
Step 1 trap — bright on T1 is not always fat

Things bright on T1: fat, gadolinium enhancement, methemoglobin (subacute blood), melanin, protein-rich fluid. Always compare pre- vs post-contrast T1 and use fat saturation before calling it fat.

Q6. FLAIR and fat saturation: how do we make the normal go dark?
  • Fluid and fat protons spin so differently from other tissue that we can "saturate" them out (make them dark) on purpose.
  • FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) = a T2-type image where normal CSF is suppressed (black).
    • Abnormal fluid (edema, gliosis, demyelination) stays bright → picked up faster than on plain T2, especially next to the ventricles.
  • FLAIR + FS (fat saturation) = normal CSF and normal fat both dark (scalp and skull marrow go black).
    • Very useful for picking up meningitis quickly: abnormal meningeal/sulcal signal stands out against a dark background.
CheckVentricles are dark, GM is brighter than WM, and scalp fat is still bright. Name the sequence.
FLAIR (without fat saturation). Dark CSF + T2-type brain = FLAIR; if the scalp fat were dark too it would be FLAIR + FS.
Step 1 HY — FLAIR in multiple sclerosis

MS plaques are T2/FLAIR hyperintense and periventricular, oriented perpendicular to the ventricles ("Dawson fingers"). Active plaques enhance with gadolinium (often an open-ring pattern).

Buzzwords — sequences
"bright ventricles" → T2"dark ventricles, T2-looking brain" → FLAIR"dark scalp fat" → fat-sat (FS)"WM brighter than GM" → T1"restricted diffusion" → DWI bright / ADC dark

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1An image shows bright white bone, dark ventricles, a grainy brain and cortex slightly brighter than white matter. Modality?
Non-contrast CT. Bright bone (bone is dark on MRI), poor soft-tissue contrast, GM hyperdense to WM.
A2A lesion is bright on T1 and turns dark when fat saturation is applied. What is it made of?
Fat (e.g., a lipoma). T1 likes fat; fat saturation removes fat signal, proving the composition.
A3Predict: on FLAIR, will a periventricular edema rim be easier or harder to see than on T2?
Easier. On T2 both CSF and edema are bright and blur together; FLAIR darkens normal CSF so the bright edema stands out.
A4A 70-year-old's CT shows the left insular cortex blending into the white matter. What does this mean?
Loss of gray–white differentiation (insular ribbon sign) → early left MCA infarct (cytotoxic edema of the cortex). Other causes of lost GM/WM differentiation: seizure, infection.

LO 2Core neuroimaging conceptsPick the study, decide on contrast, read edema, diffusion and enhancement

By the end: you can choose CT vs MRI (with or without contrast) for a given patient, explain vasogenic vs cytotoxic edema and DWI at the cell level, decide whether a lesion is intra- or extra-axial, and use signal + enhancement pattern to build a differential.
Q1. Which study should I order first?

Before ordering, answer three questions: Why am I ordering this? What do I hope it tells me? How will it change management?

FeatureCTMRI
PhysicsIonizing radiation (x-rays); densityHydrogen protons in a magnetic field; no ionizing radiation
Words usedHyper-/hypo-/isodenseHyper-/hypo-/isointense (signal)
Speed · cost · availabilityFast, cheap, everywhereSlow, expensive, needs more technologists
Safety screeningNone for metal; think radiation (children, pregnancy)Metal screening (pacemakers, clips, implants)
Soft-tissue detailPoorExcellent; definitive about lesions
Best useFirst imaging study in the CNS and for any acute process: acute hemorrhage, mass effect, hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, trauma, fracturesCharacterize a lesion (tumor, infection, demyelination), DWI for stroke, posterior fossa, cranial nerves
Contrast agentIodinated (renal caution)Gadolinium (avoid in pregnancy)
CheckA 30-year-old arrives after a motorcycle crash with GCS 9. First head study?
Non-contrast CT head: fast, no metal screening, detects acute blood, mass effect, hydrocephalus and fractures.
Step 1 HY — classic "next step" imaging
  • Acute stroke → non-contrast CT to rule out hemorrhage before thrombolysis.
  • Suspected SAH → non-contrast CT; if negative and suspicion high → LP for xanthochromia.
  • Suspected meningitis → CT before LP only if signs of ↑ICP or mass (papilledema, focal deficit, altered mental status, seizure, immunocompromise); otherwise LP + antibiotics without delay.
Step 1 trap — DWI is more sensitive, but…

MRI DWI detects ischemia within minutes, yet the first study in a suspected stroke is still non-contrast CT, because the immediate decision (tPA or not) hinges on excluding blood.

Q2. When do we add contrast, and when should we not?
  • Why contrast? To evaluate masses and suspected infection (and vessels). Contrast leaks where the blood–brain barrier is broken or vascularity is high → the lesion "enhances".
  • Why the first ER CT is non-contrast: acute blood is bright and contrast is bright → contrast can hide a subtle hemorrhage. Subtle hemorrhage suspected? → non-contrast CT.
  • Iodinated CT contrast affects renal function → check GFR first (GFR > 60 is fine). Low GFR → you cannot use CT contrast.
CT contrast (iodinated)MRI contrast (gadolinium)
Use forMass, infection, vesselsEnhancing / vascular lesions: tumor, infection, inflammation (the pattern narrows the differential)
Avoid whenSuspected hemorrhage or infarct (first study) · low GFR / high creatinine · contrast allergyPregnancy
Low GFRCannot use (affects renal function)Can be given (not nephrotoxic); it just clears more slowly
Looks likeHyperdense vessels / lesionBright on post-contrast T1 ("T1 + C", "T1 post")
CheckA 68-year-old with CKD (GFR 22) has a suspected brain mass. Can you order a contrast CT?
No. Iodinated contrast should not be given with a low GFR. Choose MRI (gadolinium can be given with low GFR in this course's teaching; it clears more slowly) or a non-contrast study.
Step 1 HY — boards phrase gadolinium differently

Boards phrase it as: gadolinium in severe renal failure (GFR < 30, dialysis) carries a risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (skin thickening, joint contractures). Iodinated contrast → contrast-induced nephropathy and allergic-type reactions (premedicate with steroids + antihistamine if prior reaction).

Memory tool — look for blood first

"Blood is bright; contrast is bright, so don't add contrast until you've looked for blood."

Step 1 trap — contrast picks

A pregnant patient with a new seizure: avoid gadolinium, not MRI itself. Non-contrast MRI (or non-contrast CT if acute) is fine.

Q3. Vasogenic vs cytotoxic edema: what is the difference?
Ischemiano ATP
→
Pump failsNa⁺ stays in cell, water follows
→
Cytotoxiccells swell · GM + WM
→
Cells burstBBB disrupted
→
Vasogenicfluid leaks into WM interstitium
FeatureVasogenicCytotoxic
MechanismBBB disrupted → fluid leaks into the interstitiumNa⁺/K⁺ pump failure → Na⁺ and water inside cells
CompartmentExtracellularIntracellular
WhereWhite matter only (finger-like; cortex spared)Gray ± white matter (GM/WM junction lost)
CourseAcute; "the brain is irritated"Acute (mass effect) or chronic (volume loss)
Cell deathNoYes
Classic causesTumor, abscess, trauma; late infarctIschemic stroke, hypoxia, ↓O₂-carrying capacity
DWINot restrictedRestricted (bright)
  • Sequence: ischemia → no ATP → Na⁺/K⁺ pump fails → Na⁺ inside cells → water follows → cytotoxic edema (GM + WM).
  • Cells keep swelling → burst → BBB disrupted → vasogenic edema (WM only).
  • An infarct always starts as cytotoxic. BBB disrupted = vasogenic.
CheckA metastasis has dark fingers of edema reaching into the white matter but the overlying cortex looks normal. Which edema?
Vasogenic: BBB leak around the tumor, confined to white matter, cortex spared.
Step 1 HY — treating edema
  • Vasogenic edema (tumor, abscess) responds to dexamethasone (tightens the BBB).
  • Cytotoxic edema (stroke) does not respond to steroids; manage ICP (elevate head, osmotherapy with mannitol / hypertonic saline, hemicraniectomy for malignant MCA edema).
  • Third type: interstitial edema from obstructive hydrocephalus (transependymal CSF flow around the ventricles).
Memory tool — V for vessel

Vasogenic = Vessel leak (BBB) → white-matter "V-shaped fingers". Cytotoxic = Cell swells → Cortex involved.

Q4. What does diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) show?
  • DWI measures how freely water molecules move in tissue. Normal brain: water wanders between cells → dark.
  • Anything that shrinks the extracellular space or thickens it restricts diffusion → bright on DWI:
    • Acute stroke: cells swell (cytotoxic edema). Bright within minutes; DWI is the most sensitive sequence for acute ischemia.
    • Tightly packed, highly cellular tumors (e.g., lymphoma, medulloblastoma).
    • Abscess: thick, viscous pus.
  • ADC map (apparent diffusion coefficient) is the "proof": true restriction = bright on DWI and dark on ADC.
  • Use DWI to evaluate stroke or cellular lesions: restricted diffusion = acute infarct (cytotoxic edema), hypercellular tumor, abscess.
  • DWI is built on a T2 image, so a very T2-bright lesion can look bright on DWI too ("T2 shine-through"); it will be bright on ADC as well.
CheckBesides cell swelling in stroke, how else can you "fill the box" so that extracellular water movement decreases?
Pack it with cells (hypercellular tumor) or with viscous fluid (abscess pus). Both are bright on DWI.
Step 1 HY — ring lesion + DWI

A ring-enhancing lesion with a DWI-bright center = abscess (pus restricts). A necrotic tumor center is usually not restricted.

Step 1 trap — shine-through

Bright DWI is not automatically stroke. Check ADC: dark ADC = true restriction; bright ADC = T2 shine-through (e.g., an old infarct or cyst).

Buzzwords — diffusion
"restricted diffusion within minutes" → acute ischemic stroke"DWI bright, ADC dark" → true restriction"bright DWI center of a ring" → abscess
Q5. Is the lesion intra-axial or extra-axial?

Intra-axial

  • Inside the brain parenchyma, enclosed by the pia mater (which hugs the brain surface)
  • Most tumors and infections
  • Most common intra-axial mass: glioma (primary brain tumor)
  • Bleeds: intraparenchymal hemorrhage, contusion, diffuse axonal injury

Extra-axial

  • Outside the pia: epidural, subdural, subarachnoid spaces
  • Most common extra-axial mass: meningioma
  • Bleeds: epidural, subdural, subarachnoid

Signs a mass is extra-axial

  • Definitive: something interposed between brain and lesion: a CSF cleft, vessels, cortex, or dura.
  • Suggestive: broad base along the calvarium, overlying bone change (hyperostosis), enhancement of adjacent meninges (dural tail), brain displaced away from the skull (white matter buckling).
CheckA dural-based mass with a CSF cleft between it and the cortex and an enhancing dural tail. Location and likely diagnosis?
Extra-axial → meningioma. The CSF cleft is a definitive extra-axial sign; the dural tail is suggestive.
Step 1 HY — meningioma and brain tumor epidemiology
  • Meningioma: arachnoid cap cells, women, dural-based, dural tail, psammoma bodies, whorls; associated with NF2 and prior radiation.
  • Boards: the most common brain tumors overall in adults are metastases (multiple, at the gray–white junction; lung, breast, melanoma, kidney); the most common malignant primary is glioblastoma.
Step 1 trap — the subarachnoid space is extra-axial

SAH sits in the sulci right against the brain, but it is still outside the pia → extra-axial. Contusion and DAI are intra-axial.

Q6. What is this lesion made of? Match it to a reference tissue on every sequence

The trick: pick a reference you know (CSF, scalp fat) and ask whether the lesion behaves like it on every sequence. If it behaves like CSF, it is CSF.

Lesion contentT1T2FLAIR / FLAIR + FS
Simple CSF (porencephalic cyst)DarkBrightDark (CSF suppressed)
Fat (lipoma)BrightIntermediate (less than fluid)Dark on FS
Edema / abnormal fluidDarkBrightStays bright on FLAIR
CheckA lesion is dark T1, bright T2, and bright on FLAIR. Simple CSF cyst?
No. Simple CSF would be suppressed (dark) on FLAIR. Bright FLAIR means abnormal fluid (edema, gliosis, proteinaceous fluid, tumor).
Memory tool — follow the reference

"If it walks like CSF on T1, T2 and FLAIR, it is CSF." "If it vanishes with fat-sat, it was fat."

Q7. How does the enhancement pattern narrow the differential?

On post-contrast images, all white areas are abnormal enhancement (high vascularity or BBB breakdown); the pattern of enhancement helps narrow the differential diagnosis. The shape of the enhancement matters because each pattern has a different differential.

PatternWhat enhancesThink
LeptomeningealPia-arachnoid, follows sulci and cerebellar foliaMeningitis, leptomeningeal carcinomatosis, sarcoid
PachymeningealDura, smooth along the inner skullIntracranial hypotension, post-surgery, dural metastases
Cortical gyral & periventricularGyri / ependymaSubacute infarct, encephalitis, ventriculitis
Subcortical nodularSmall dots at the gray–white junctionMetastases, septic emboli
Dural tailBroad dural-based mass + tapering duraMeningioma (extra-axial)
Smooth open (incomplete) ringRing open toward the cortexDemyelination (tumefactive MS)
Smooth closed ringThin, complete ringAbscess, metastasis
Necrotic (thick, irregular) ringShaggy ring around necrosisGlioblastoma, necrotic metastasis

Build the differential with a fixed list, then narrow it with signal, enhancement and DWI: Infarct · Mass · Hemorrhage · Infection · Toxic/metabolic · Vascular · Degenerative.

CheckA ring lesion is open on its cortical side. Most likely category?
Demyelination (open-ring sign), rather than abscess or tumor, which form closed rings.
Step 1 HY — ring-enhancing lesions

MAGICAL DR: Metastasis, Abscess, Glioblastoma, Infarct (subacute), Contusion, AIDS (toxoplasmosis, lymphoma), Lymphoma, Demyelination, Radiation necrosis.

  • AIDS (CD4 < 100): multiple ring lesions in the basal ganglia → toxoplasmosis; single periventricular lesion, EBV-positive CSF → primary CNS lymphoma.
Memory tool — lepto vs pachy

Lepto = "thin" membranes that dip into the sulci (pia-arachnoid). Pachy = "thick" dura that stays smooth against the skull.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A patient with an older, non-MRI-safe pacemaker needs evaluation of a suspected brain mass. GFR is 85. Which study?
CT with IV contrast. MRI is unsafe; contrast CT is indicated for a mass, and renal function is normal.
A2A pregnant woman at 20 weeks has a first seizure and needs a brain MRI. What do you leave out?
Gadolinium. It is contraindicated in pregnancy; do a non-contrast MRI.
A3Predict the DWI and ADC appearance of a brain abscess center versus a simple porencephalic cyst.
Abscess pus: DWI bright, ADC dark (restricted). Cyst: DWI dark, ADC bright (free water). Pus is viscous; CSF is not.
A4One lesion enhances, is surrounded by T2-bright white matter, and is DWI-bright. Another follows CSF on every sequence. Which is more worrying?
The first. Enhancement (BBB breakdown) + vasogenic edema + restricted diffusion (high cellularity) points to tumor or abscess. The second is a benign CSF cyst.
A5A 3-day-old infarct now shows edema spreading through the white matter. Why can a stroke cause vasogenic edema later?
The infarct starts cytotoxic; as swollen cells die and burst, the BBB breaks down and fluid leaks into the white matter interstitium = vasogenic edema.

LO 3Basic intracranial pathologyBleeds, strokes, mass effect, meninges and a mass

By the end: you can name each hemorrhage by its shape and space, date blood on CT and MRI, spot an acute infarct on CT and DWI, call mass effect and herniation, and work through an enhancing mass or meningeal case to a diagnosis and next step.
Q1. Something is bright on a non-contrast CT. Which of the four hemorrhages is it?

Start from the layers. The space the blood is in decides its shape, and the shape gives the diagnosis.

TypeAxial locationCT shapeVessel / causeClassic clinical story
EpiduralExtra-axial (skull ↔ dura)Lens / biconvex; does not cross sutures (dura is stuck there); can cross the falx/tentoriumMiddle meningeal artery; temporal bone (pterion) fractureYoung trauma patient, brief LOC → lucid interval → rapid decline
SubduralExtra-axial (dura ↔ arachnoid)Crescent along the convexity; crosses sutures, not the midline falxTorn bridging veins; blunt head traumaElderly (atrophy), alcohol use, anticoagulation, shaken baby; gradual confusion
SubarachnoidExtra-axial (under arachnoid)Blood in sulci and basal cisternsAneurysm rupture or trauma; ADPKD association"Worst headache of my life", neck stiffness
IntraparenchymalIntra-axial (within pia)Bright blob in brain tissue ± surrounding edemaHypertension (Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms)Hypertensive patient with sudden deficit; putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum
CheckAn 80-year-old on warfarin falls and becomes progressively confused over a day. CT: hyperdense crescent along the left convexity crossing suture lines. Diagnosis?
Acute subdural hematoma (extra-axial): torn bridging veins; atrophy + anticoagulation are risk factors.
Step 1 HY — epidural vs subdural
  • Epidural: arterial (middle meningeal a., branch of maxillary a.), lens, does not cross sutures, lucid interval, can cause rapid uncal herniation → emergency evacuation.
  • Subdural: venous (bridging veins), crescent, crosses sutures, slower. Shaken baby = SDH + retinal hemorrhages.
  • Hypertensive bleeds: putamen (most common), thalamus, pons, cerebellum. Lobar bleeds in the elderly → cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
Memory tool — lens vs crescent
  • Epidural = lEns; Arterial; stops at sutures because dura is "glued" there.
  • Subdural = Sickle (crescent); Slow venous ooze; Senior citizens.
Step 1 trap — sutures vs falx

Epidural blood is limited by sutures but can cross the midline (above the sinus); subdural blood crosses sutures but is stopped by the falx/tentorium. Don't swap them.

Buzzwords — bleeds
"lucid interval" → epidural"biconvex / lens-shaped" → epidural"crescent crossing sutures" → subdural"elderly, alcoholic, fall" → subdural"thunderclap / worst headache" → SAH"hypertensive, putamen" → intraparenchymal
Q2. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: how do I work it up and what goes wrong next?
Thunderclap headache"worst of my life", meningismus, ↓consciousness
→
Non-contrast CTblood in sulci / cisterns (most sensitive in first ~6 h)
→
CT negative?LP: xanthochromia (bilirubin), RBCs that do not clear
→
CT angiographyfind the aneurysm → coil or clip
  • Causes: overall most common = trauma; most common non-traumatic = ruptured berry (saccular) aneurysm, usually at the anterior communicating artery.
  • Associations: ADPKD, Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan, coarctation, smoking, hypertension.
  • Complications: rebleeding (first day), vasospasm with delayed ischemia (~3–10 days; prevent with nimodipine), communicating hydrocephalus (blood blocks arachnoid granulations), hyponatremia (SIADH / cerebral salt wasting).
CheckA 55-year-old with a family history of polycystic kidney disease has a sudden severe headache, BP 180/100. CT: hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns. Diagnosis?
Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (ruptured berry aneurysm). ADPKD is a classic association.
Step 1 HY — aneurysm localization
  • ACom aneurysm: most common; can compress the optic chiasm → bitemporal visual field defect.
  • PCom aneurysm: CN III palsy with a blown pupil (parasympathetic fibers run on the outside of the nerve).
Step 1 trap — negative CT

A negative CT does not exclude SAH when the headache started many hours ago. Next step is LP, not discharge and not MRI.

Q3. How old is this blood? (CT and MRI)
Stage (time)Blood productT1T2
Hyperacute (< 1 day)OxyhemoglobinIsoBright
Acute (1–3 days)DeoxyhemoglobinIsoDark
Early subacute (3–7 days)Intracellular methemoglobinBrightDark
Late subacute (1–4 weeks)Extracellular methemoglobinBrightBright
Chronic (> 1 month)Hemosiderin (rim)DarkDark
CheckA 2-week-old subdural is barely visible on CT. Why, and what helps?
It is subacute and isodense to brain. Look for indirect signs (effaced sulci, midline shift, buckled gray–white junction), or use MRI (extracellular methemoglobin is bright on T1 and T2).
Memory tool — "It Be, Iddy Biddy, BaBy, Doo Doo"

T1/T2 pairs in order: Iso/Bright → Iso/Dark → Bright/Dark → Bright/Bright → Dark/Dark. Products: oxyHb → deoxyHb → intracellular metHb → extracellular metHb → hemosiderin.

Step 1 HY — hemosiderin "blooms"

Susceptibility sequences (GRE/SWI) make hemosiderin and calcium look black and larger ("blooming"). Many tiny lobar microbleeds in an elderly patient → cerebral amyloid angiopathy; at the gray–white junction after trauma → diffuse axonal injury.

Step 1 trap — isodense subdural

"Normal" CT in a confused elderly patient 2–3 weeks after a fall can hide an isodense subacute SDH. Look for asymmetric sulci and midline shift.

Q4. How does an ischemic stroke look on CT and on DWI?
  • Cause: lack of blood supply or ↓ oxygen-carrying capacity.
  • CT of an acute stroke: hypodense territory, hydrocephalus, midline shift → then ask what the presenting symptoms are.
  • Presentation: contralateral extremity weakness/numbness, aphasia (dominant, usually left hemisphere), dysarthria, facial palsy, altered mental status.
  • MCA is the most commonly occluded artery (largest territory). MCA pattern: face and arm > leg.
  • Every infarct starts as cytotoxic edema; later, burst cells and BBB breakdown add vasogenic edema.
Time after onsetNon-contrast CTMRI
Minutes to 6 hOften normal · hyperdense MCA sign (clot)DWI bright / ADC dark within minutes
6–24 hLoss of GM/WM differentiation, insular ribbon sign, obscured lentiform nucleusFLAIR becomes bright
Days 2–5Wedge of hypodensity in a vascular territory; swelling peaks → mass effect, herniation riskDWI still bright
Weeks to monthsCSF-dark encephalomalacia, volume loss, ex vacuo ventricular enlargementGliosis; DWI fades (ADC normalizes then rises)
  • Several small DWI-bright foci that are bilateral, anterior and posterior, supra- and infratentorial → multiple vascular territories at once → embolic source (heart, e.g., atrial fibrillation; or the proximal aorta).
  • DWI + symptoms: acute aphasia + right-sided weakness/numbness + altered mental status = acute left MCA infarct.
  • Differential for multiple DWI-bright foci: acute infarcts (embolic) · hypercellular tumors · abscesses. The vascular-territory pattern and clinical picture favor emboli.
CheckSudden left hemiplegia 1 hour ago. CT parenchyma looks nearly normal, but the right MCA is bright. What is this?
Hyperdense MCA sign: acute thrombus is denser than flowing blood. Suggests a large-vessel occlusion → CTA, consider thrombectomy (and tPA if no blood and in window).
Step 1 HY — acute stroke management
  • Non-contrast CT first to exclude hemorrhage → IV thrombolysis (alteplase/tenecteplase) within 4.5 h of last known well.
  • Mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion, up to 24 h in selected patients.
  • Dominant (left) MCA → aphasia; non-dominant (right) MCA → hemineglect. Eyes deviate toward the lesion.
  • Cerebral cortex neurons: red neurons at 12–24 h; liquefactive necrosis.
Step 1 trap — normal early CT

A normal CT in the first hours does not rule out ischemic stroke. And a bright DWI spot is not always stroke: hypercellular tumors and abscesses restrict too.

Buzzwords — stroke imaging
"hyperdense MCA sign" → acute MCA thrombus"insular ribbon sign" → early MCA infarct"wedge-shaped hypodensity in a vascular territory" → infarct"multiple territories on DWI" → embolic
Q5. What do mass effect, midline shift, hydrocephalus and herniation look like?
  • Reading a stroke CT: name all three findings (acute stroke, hydrocephalus, midline shift), then ask what symptoms the patient presented with.
  • Mass effect: anything taking up space (bleed, tumor, swollen infarct) effaces sulci and ventricles, loses the "smile", and flattens the 4th ventricle "frown".
  • Midline shift: the septum pellucidum and falx are pushed to the opposite side.
  • Hydrocephalus: enlarged ventricles. A shifted brain can trap the opposite lateral ventricle at the foramen of Monro → it dilates (non-communicating). SAH and meningitis block arachnoid granulations → communicating hydrocephalus.
CheckA patient with a large right epidural hematoma develops a fixed, dilated right pupil. Which herniation?
Right uncal (transtentorial) herniation: the uncus compresses the ipsilateral CN III; parasympathetic fibers on its surface are hit first → blown pupil.
Step 1 HY — uncal herniation triad
  • Ipsilateral dilated pupil / ptosis (CN III).
  • Contralateral homonymous hemianopia (PCA compression).
  • Ipsilateral hemiparesis = Kernohan notch (opposite crus pressed against the tentorium), a false localizing sign. Usual hemiparesis is contralateral (ipsilateral crus).
Step 1 trap — hemiparesis on the "wrong" side

Weakness on the same side as the mass does not move the lesion; it signals Kernohan phenomenon.

Memory tool — top to bottom

Herniations go across (subfalcine), over (uncal), down (central), out (tonsillar). The lower it goes, the closer to the breathing center in the medulla.

Q6. Fever, headache and the meninges: what does contrast show, and why does history matter?

56-year-old · 3 days of headache, fever, N/V

Leptomeningeal enhancement → meningitis. Next step: LP.

56-year-old · lung cancer · 3 days of headache, N/V

Same image → leptomeningeal carcinomatosis. Next step: LP (cytology).

Same pattern, different disease. Your history and physical decide the diagnosis; the image narrows the differential.

CheckFebrile patient, neck stiffness, unremarkable CT. Which MRI approach shows meningeal disease best?
FLAIR + FS (normal CSF and fat suppressed) and post-contrast T1, looking for abnormal sulcal signal and leptomeningeal enhancement. Then LP.
Step 1 HY — meningitis and imaging

Imaging is often normal in bacterial meningitis; CSF is the diagnosis. Get CT before LP only when ↑ICP / mass is possible. Leptomeningeal enhancement predominantly at the basal cisterns → think TB (or fungal) meningitis.

Q7. Putting it together: a slowly growing mass

Case. A 56-year-old woman has months of slowly worsening headaches and altered mental status. First study? Non-contrast CT: something is pushing on the ventricles, bilateral but contiguous, with vasogenic edema. CT does not give enough information → contrast-enhanced MRI.

SequenceFindingWhat it means
T2Lesion hypointense, crossing the corpus callosum; bright surrounding WMDensely cellular (little free water); vasogenic edema
T1HypointenseNot fat, not subacute blood
T1 + contrastDiffuse homogeneous enhancementBBB breakdown; solid (not necrotic) tumor
DWIMild restricted diffusionHypercellular

Run the list: infarct · mass · hemorrhage · infection · toxic/metabolic · vascular · degenerative → Mass: primary CNS lymphoma.

Primary CNS lymphoma homogeneous

Periventricular, crosses corpus callosum, T2 dark, DWI bright, homogeneous enhancement (ring-like in AIDS). B-cell (DLBCL); EBV in AIDS.

Glioblastoma necrotic ring

"Butterfly" across the corpus callosum, thick irregular ring around necrosis, hemorrhage; pseudopalisading necrosis; GFAP+.

Metastases multiple

Multiple, round, at the gray–white junction, lots of vasogenic edema for their size. Lung, breast, melanoma, renal.

Abscess smooth ring

Thin smooth ring, DWI-bright center (pus), edema; fever; spread from sinus/ear, dental, endocarditis.

Toxoplasmosis AIDS

Multiple ring lesions in the basal ganglia / gray–white junction, CD4 < 100. Treat empirically; shrinks in ~2 weeks.

Meningioma extra-axial

Dural-based, dural tail, CSF cleft, hyperostosis, homogeneous enhancement.

CheckWhy is a mass that is dark on T2 and bright on DWI more likely lymphoma than glioblastoma?
Lymphoma is densely packed with cells (high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, little free water) → T2 dark + restricted diffusion + homogeneous enhancement. GBM usually has a necrotic center and a thick irregular ring.
Step 1 HY — primary CNS lymphoma
  • Usually diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; in AIDS it is EBV-driven (EBV DNA in CSF).
  • Single periventricular lesion in AIDS → lymphoma; multiple basal ganglia lesions → toxoplasmosis.
  • Steroids can make it shrink or vanish → biopsy before steroids if possible.
Step 1 trap — crossing the corpus callosum

Two tumors classically cross the corpus callosum: GBM (necrotic "butterfly") and lymphoma (homogeneous, DWI bright). Use the enhancement pattern and diffusion to separate them.

ApplyLO 3 application questions

A1A 22-year-old is hit in the temple by a baseball, talks normally for an hour, then becomes unresponsive. Predict the CT.
Biconvex (lens) hyperdense epidural hematoma over the temporal region, not crossing sutures, from a torn middle meningeal artery. Classic lucid interval.
A2DWI shows multiple small bright foci in both hemispheres and the cerebellum. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Mechanism?
Cardioembolic infarcts: emboli scatter to several vascular territories (bilateral, anterior and posterior circulation).
A3Day 3 after a large right MCA stroke, the patient becomes drowsy and the right pupil dilates. What happened on imaging?
Peak cytotoxic swelling ("malignant MCA edema") → midline shift and right uncal herniation compressing CN III. Consider decompressive hemicraniectomy.
A4MRI of a hemorrhage is bright on both T1 and T2. Roughly how old is it?
Late subacute (about 1–4 weeks): extracellular methemoglobin ("BaBy").
A5A patient with AIDS (CD4 40) has several ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia. Most likely diagnosis and next step?
Toxoplasmosis: start empiric pyrimethamine–sulfadiazine (+ leucovorin) and reimage in ~2 weeks; biopsy if no response (think lymphoma).

IMGImage ID drillName the modality, sequence and finding, then tap to check

How to use: for each image say (1) CT or MRI, (2) which sequence(s), (3) the finding, (4) the next step if relevant. Then open the card.
1 · Two scans, same patient. What changed? (tap for answer)
Non-contrast CT (left) vs contrast CT (right). Vessels and dural sinuses are bright after iodinated contrast. Used for a suspected mass or infection, only with a normal GFR.
2 · Which sequence is each? (tap for answer)
Left = T1 (CSF dark, WM brighter than GM). Right = T2 (CSF bright, GM brighter than WM).
3 · Name the three sequences (tap for answer)
FLAIR (CSF dark, T2-type brain) · T2 (CSF bright) · FLAIR + FS (CSF and fat dark; scalp black).
4 · Three non-contrast CTs: name each bleed (tap for answer)
Intraparenchymal (hypertension; intra-axial) · acute subdural (crescent; blunt trauma) · subarachnoid (blood in sulci; aneurysm or trauma; ADPKD).
5 · Acute aphasia + right weakness. Findings? (tap for answer)
Acute left MCA infarct (hypodense, swollen; cytotoxic edema) with midline shift and hydrocephalus of the trapped opposite ventricle. Right image = normal reference.
6 · What is this lesion made of? (tap for answer)
T1 dark · T2 bright · FLAIR dark = follows CSF on every sequence → porencephalic (CSF) cyst.
7 · T1 · T1 + C · T2 · FLAIR + FS. Diagnosis? (tap for answer)
Bright T1, no real enhancement, duller than fluid on T2, dark with fat saturation → lipoma.
8 · DWI at four levels. Findings and mechanism? (tap for answer)
Multiple foci of restricted diffusion, bilateral, anterior and posterior, supra- and infratentorial → acute embolic infarcts (differential: hypercellular tumors, abscesses).
9 · Post-contrast MRI, fever + headache (right = normal) (tap for answer)
Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement → meningitis (or carcinomatosis if known cancer). Next step: LP.
10 · T2 · T1 · T1 + post · DWI. Diagnosis? (tap for answer)
T2-dark mass crossing the corpus callosum, vasogenic edema, homogeneous enhancement, mild restricted diffusion → primary CNS lymphoma.

MCQPractice questionsClick an answer to see the explanation.

Score: 0 / 0

1A 19-year-old is struck on the side of the head during a lacrosse game. He loses consciousness briefly, then talks normally on the sideline for 45 minutes before becoming drowsy and vomiting. Non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense biconvex collection over the left temporal lobe that stops at the coronal suture. Which vessel is most likely injured?

C. Middle meningeal artery. Lens-shaped, suture-limited blood + lucid interval = epidural hematoma from a pterion/temporal fracture tearing the MMA. Bridging veins (A) → subdural crescent. ACom (B) → SAH. Lenticulostriates (D) → hypertensive putaminal bleed. Sinus injury (E) is uncommon and not lens-shaped.

2A 74-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has become more confused over 3 days after a fall. Non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense crescentic collection along the right convexity that crosses the coronal suture but does not cross the falx. Which space contains the blood?

A. Subdural space. Crescent crossing sutures, stopped by the falx, elderly + alcohol (atrophy stretches bridging veins) = subdural hematoma. Skull–dura (B) = epidural lens. Arachnoid–pia (C) = SAH in sulci. Parenchyma (D) = intra-axial bleed. Ventricle (E) = intraventricular hemorrhage.

3A 48-year-old woman has a sudden, severe occipital headache that began 14 hours ago while lifting weights. She has neck stiffness but no focal deficits. Non-contrast head CT is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

E. Lumbar puncture. Thunderclap headache = SAH until proven otherwise. CT sensitivity falls after ~6 hours, so a negative CT needs LP for xanthochromia / persistent RBCs, then CTA. Discharge (A) misses a rebleed risk. Contrast CT (B) and gadolinium MRI (C) do not replace LP. Alteplase (D) is for ischemic stroke and is dangerous in SAH.

4A 67-year-old woman is brought in 50 minutes after the sudden onset of right arm and face weakness and difficulty finding words. BP is 168/94 and glucose is normal. Which imaging study should be performed first?

B. Non-contrast CT. Fast and available; its job is to exclude hemorrhage before thrombolysis. DWI (A) is more sensitive for ischemia but slower and not needed to give tPA. Contrast CT (C) can hide blood. Carotid ultrasound (D) is part of the later workup. Catheter angiography (E) is invasive and follows CTA for thrombectomy.

5A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation develops sudden left hemiparesis. MRI 2 hours later shows a region in the right MCA territory that is bright on diffusion-weighted imaging and dark on the ADC map. What is the primary cellular mechanism of this signal?

D. Cytotoxic edema. No ATP → pump failure → Na⁺ and water enter cells → extracellular space shrinks → restricted diffusion (DWI bright, ADC dark). BBB leak (A) is vasogenic edema (not restricted). Hemosiderin (B) is chronic blood. Obstructed CSF (C) gives interstitial edema. Gliosis (E) occurs weeks later.

6An MRI obtained for headaches shows a well-circumscribed parenchymal lesion that is hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, and completely suppressed (dark) on FLAIR. It does not enhance. What is the lesion most likely composed of?

A. CSF (e.g., porencephalic cyst): it follows CSF on every sequence. Fat (B) would be T1 bright. Edema (C) stays bright on FLAIR. Methemoglobin (D) is T1 bright. Dense tumor (E) would be T2 dark/intermediate and usually enhance.

7A 29-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation has her first generalized seizure. She is now alert with a normal neurologic exam. An outpatient brain MRI is planned. Which component of a standard protocol should be omitted?

C. Gadolinium is contraindicated in pregnancy (crosses the placenta). Non-contrast sequences (A, B, D, E) involve no ionizing radiation and no contrast and are acceptable.

8A radiology resident is shown an axial brain MRI in which the cortex is brighter than the white matter, the lateral ventricles are black, and the scalp and skull marrow are also black. Which sequence is this?

E. FLAIR + FS. GM > WM means a T2-based image; dark CSF means FLAIR; dark scalp fat and marrow mean fat saturation. T1 (A, D) shows WM brighter than GM and bright fat. T2 (B) has bright CSF. Plain FLAIR (C) keeps scalp fat bright.

9A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV (CD4 count 45/mm³) has fever, headache and left-sided weakness. Contrast MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and at the gray–white junction with surrounding edema. Which is the most likely cause?

D. Toxoplasmosis: multiple ring-enhancing lesions, basal ganglia, CD4 < 100. Lymphoma (A) is usually single, periventricular, EBV+. PML (B) = non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect. GBM (C) is a single necrotic "butterfly" mass. Cryptococcus (E) causes meningitis with gelatinous pseudocysts, not multiple rings.

10A 63-year-old immunocompetent woman has 3 months of personality change and headaches. MRI shows a periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum that is hypointense on T2, enhances homogeneously and intensely, and shows restricted diffusion. There is no central necrosis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

C. Primary CNS lymphoma: densely cellular (T2 dark, DWI bright), homogeneous enhancement, crosses the corpus callosum. GBM (A) also crosses but has a thick necrotic ring. Meningioma (B) is extra-axial with a dural tail. Abscess (D) has a smooth ring with a DWI-bright center. MS (E) is T2 bright, often an open ring.

11A 59-year-old woman with breast cancer has a 2-cm enhancing metastasis in the right parietal lobe. Non-contrast CT shows extensive finger-like hypodensity extending through the adjacent white matter while the overlying cortex is preserved. Which best explains this hypodensity?

A. Vasogenic edema: leaky tumor vessels break the BBB; fluid tracks along white matter and spares the cortex; treat with dexamethasone. Pump failure (B) = cytotoxic edema involving cortex. Transependymal flow (C) is periventricular. Hemorrhage (D) would be hyperdense. Liquefactive necrosis (E) follows infarction.

12A 76-year-old man arrives 70 minutes after sudden left hemiplegia and right gaze deviation. Non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage and preserved gray–white differentiation, but a linear bright density in the proximal right middle cerebral artery. What does this finding represent?

E. Hyperdense MCA sign: fresh clot is denser than flowing blood. It precedes parenchymal changes and points to a large-vessel occlusion → CTA and thrombectomy (± tPA). Calcified plaque (A) is denser and patchy. SAH (B) fills sulci and cisterns. No contrast was given (C). Insular edema (D) is hypodense (insular ribbon loss).

13A 35-year-old man with a large left temporal epidural hematoma becomes less responsive. His left pupil is dilated and nonreactive, and he has weakness of the left arm and leg. Which best explains the motor finding?

B. Kernohan notch. Uncal herniation shifts the brainstem so the contralateral (right) crus is pressed against the tentorium → ipsilateral (left) hemiparesis, a false-localizing sign. The blown left pupil is ipsilateral CN III. ACA compression (A) gives contralateral leg weakness. Tonsillar herniation (C) causes respiratory arrest. PCA infarct (D) causes a visual field cut. Left cortex compression (E) would cause right-sided weakness.
